extracted.intended_audience: companies that develop or market consumer-facing AI products, in-house counsel, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how businesses should substantiate and present performance claims about consumer-facing AI models to avoid FTC enforcement; focuses on evidentiary, recordkeeping, and post-order compliance obligations. Useful to legal/compliance teams preparing advertising and product documentation for AI tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and non-misleading representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannot make any representations about the effectiveness of any covered product unless it is not misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising must not overstate a product's capabilities (e.g., advertising '98 percent' accuracy when independent testing shows much lower rates). The proposed FTC order bars false, misleading, or unsupported advertising about AI product effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent and reliable evidence supporting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Company must possess competent and reliable evidence demonstrating that the model performs as depicted before making effectiveness claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC explicitly requires 'competent and reliable' evidence at the time the claim is made; vague or tenuous testing does not suffice. The page cites Workado's claim of 98% accuracy vs independent testing showing ~53% as an example of unsupported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must be relevant to claimed use cases and domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance claims must be supported by testing and training that are representative of the real-world content and use-cases the claim targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workado's model was trained/fine-tuned to classify academic content, yet the company promoted it for general-purpose content — the FTC found this mismatch led to misleading claims. Do not generalize results from a narrow domain (e.g., academic content) to the general internet without representative testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing and training disclosures expected in evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for competent and reliable evidence will likely require information about the testing and training of the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation should include how models were trained/fine-tuned, what datasets were used, testing methodologies, metrics, sample sizes, and how those datasets map to the marketed use. The article notes regulators are still developing precise standards but will look for testing/training information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must retain any evidence they use to support efficacy or performance claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the proposed order, Workado must keep the evidence that underpins claims. Retention supports audits, enforcement inquiries, and demonstrates compliance if challenged by the FTC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for evidence (evidence must exist when claim is made)
rubrics_metrics.description: A company must have competent and reliable evidence to support a claim at the time the claim is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed order stresses that evidence must preexist the advertisement/representation — retrospective or speculative testing conducted after making claims may not cure prior misrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on deceptive AI-enabled business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC will act against AI-powered frauds, scams, or deceptive uses of AI that mislead consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of enforcement sweeps (e.g., Operation AI Comply), the FTC targeted companies misrepresenting AI capabilities (examples: DoNotPay, Sitejabber). Firms should avoid AI-enabled misrepresentations beyond strictly efficacy claims (e.g., falsely representing reviews or legal capabilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-order consumer notification obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If subject to a consent order, companies may be required to notify eligible consumers about the consent order and settlement with the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Workado proposed order requires the company to email eligible consumers about the consent order — include consumer-notification plans in compliance preparation where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing compliance reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consent orders can require periodic compliance reports to the FTC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workado must submit four annual compliance reports beginning one year after the order is issued; companies should be prepared to monitor and report compliance over multiple years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil penalties for future violations of consent orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Each future violation of a consent order may result in civil penalties (example amount noted in the order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Workado proposed order did not include a monetary component up front, the FTC warned that future violations could carry civil penalties (the page cites up to $53,088 per violation under the relevant statute). Firms should account for financial exposure in compliance risk assessments.
